extracted.intended_audience: graduate students or advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions and fundamental properties of the intersection product of line bundles with coherent sheaves/subvarieties on n-dimensional varieties, and the special case of intersection theory on surfaces; includes key propositions, exercises, and examples used to compute intersection numbers and prove basic results (multilinearity, symmetry, projection formula, asymptotic Riemann–Roch, adjunction, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: intersection product (L1,...,Ln) with F
rubrics_metrics.description: For a k-variety X, a coherent sheaf F with proper support of dimension ≤ n, and invertible sheaves L1,...,Ln on X, define (L1 ··· Ln · F) as the signed sum over the 2^n subsets S ⊂ {1,...,n} of (−1)^{|S|} χ(X, (⊗_{i∉S} Li^∨) ⊗ F). In practice one often takes F = O_Y for a closed subscheme Y and writes (L1 ··· Ln · Y), and if all Li are the same L one often writes (L^n · Y) (with a caution that L^n does not mean tensor power notation confusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central definition (20.1.1.1). Keep track of parentheses and the condition dim Supp F ≤ n. Typical useful case: F = O_Y where Y is a closed subscheme of dimension ≤ n. The definition interpolates between degree on curves and Bézout in projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with degree on curves and Bézout
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a projective curve and L an invertible sheaf, then (L · X) = deg_X L. If X = P^N and Y ⊂ X is an n-dimensional subvariety, then for generally chosen hypersurfaces H1,...,Hn of degrees d1,...,dn with 0-dimensional intersection, deg(H1 ∩ ... ∩ Hn ∩ Y) = d1·...·dn·deg(Y), and (OX(H1) · ... · OX(Hn) · Y) = d1·...·dn·deg(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.1.B: shows the intersection product recovers classical notions (degree on curves, Bézout) and motivates its interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection with effective Cartier divisors / restriction formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If D is an effective Cartier divisor on X that restricts to an effective Cartier divisor D|_Y on Y (i.e., remains locally a nonzerodivisor on Y), then (L1 · ... · Ln−1 · O(D) · Y) = (L1 · ... · Ln−1 · (D|_Y)). More generally, if D is effective and does not contain any associated point of F, then (L1 · ... · Ln−1 · O(D) · F) = (L1 · ... · Ln−1 · (F|_D)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.1.C: used to reduce dimension in computations; useful in relating intersections of line bundles to intersections of divisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation under field extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection product is preserved by extension of the base field k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.1.D: allows one to assume k is infinite or algebraically closed when proving properties of the intersection product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry and multilinearity of the intersection product
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed F, (L1 · ... · Ln · F) is a symmetric multilinear function of the Li (Proposition 20.1.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: reduce to k infinite, induct on n, use very ample line bundles and the trick of writing arbitrary line bundles as differences of very ample ones; see Exercises 20.1.E–20.1.G. Also note vanishing statements used in the proof (Exercise 20.1.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing for too many line bundles (dimension bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: If dim Supp F < n+1, then the intersection product of n+1 invertible sheaves with F vanishes (i.e., (L1 · ... · L_{n+1} · F) = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.1.H: an extension of multilinearity arguments; used in proving asymptotic polynomiality and other properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence only on numerical equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: If L1 is numerically equivalent to L1', then for arbitrary L2,...,Ln and F, (L1 · L2 · ... · Ln · F) = (L1' · L2 · ... · Ln · F); i.e., the intersection product depends only on the numerical equivalence classes of the Li (Proposition 20.1.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses reduction to the very ample case and induction on n via restriction to effective Cartier divisors missing associated points of F (Exercise 20.1.C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic Riemann–Roch (leading coefficient identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective of dimension n and F a coherent sheaf with dim Supp F ≤ n, then χ(X, L^{⊗m} ⊗ F) is a polynomial in m of degree ≤ n, and the coefficient of m^n is (L^n · F)/n! (Exercise 20.1.I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vanishing of (L^{n+1} · F) and expand the definition to get a recursion for χ; parallels the proof of Hilbert polynomial polynomiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula for intersection numbers (finite dominant case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X1 → X2 is a projective morphism of integral projective schemes of the same dimension n and L1,...,Ln are invertible sheaves on X2, then (π^*L1 · ... · π^*Ln)_{X1} = deg(X1/X2)·(L1 · ... · Ln)_{X2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.1.J: reduce to very ample case and choose sections lying over an open where π is finite flat of constant degree; handle non-dominant (degree 0) separately. A more general projection formula involving coherent sheaves is discussed in 20.1.6 / Remark (π_* and pullback interactions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity with ample line bundles (Nakai–Moishezon direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a projective k-variety and L is ample, then for any subvariety Y ⊂ X of dimension n, (L^n · Y) > 0 (Exercise 20.1.K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This direction is immediate from very ampleness and degree in projective embeddings; Nakai–Moishezon criterion (Theorem 20.4.1) asserts this characterizes ampleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomological/topological interpretation over C
rubrics_metrics.description: When k = C, (L1 · ... · Ln · Y) equals ⟨ c1(L1_an) ∪ ... ∪ c1(Ln_an), [Y_an] ⟩ in H^{2n}(Y_an, Z) ≅ Z; i.e., intersection numbers correspond to cup-products of first Chern classes on complex analytic varieties (20.1.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by multilinearity and reduction to effective Cartier divisors where c1 of the line bundle is Poincaré dual to the analytic divisor; then use induction on dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additive notation convention for line bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: By convention, tensor product of invertible sheaves is written additively to exploit multilinearity of the intersection product (Remark 20.1.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: this is a notational convenience and can cause confusion; divisors are sometimes used to avoid confusion since divisors add when line bundles tensor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface case: equivalent descriptions of intersection number for curves
rubrics_metrics.description: On a regular projective surface X, for effective divisors (curves) C and D one has several equivalent descriptions of the intersection number C·D: (i) deg_C OX(D)|_C, (ii) deg_D OX(C)|_D, (iii) Euler-characteristic formulations (χ-related), and (iv) when C and D have no common components, C·D = h^0(C ∩ D, O_{C∩D}) (Exercise/Definition 20.2.A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each description has pros and cons: (iii) (Euler characteristic) is useful algebraically, (i)/(ii) connect to line bundle degrees, and (iv) gives a local scheme-theoretic (length/h0) interpretation for intersection multiplicities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local interpretation / multiplicity via scheme-theoretic intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: If C and D have no irreducible component in common, then C·D equals the length (h^0) of the scheme-theoretic intersection C ∩ D, viewed locally as a 0-dimensional scheme (20.2.0.4 and discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to compute ordinary multiplicities (e.g., curve y − x^2 meets the x-axis with multiplicity 2). This is the local viewpoint useful in explicit algebraic computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection form on Picard group and quadratic growth of χ
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective surface X, the intersection number induces a bilinear intersection form Pic X × Pic X → Z (20.2.3.1), and χ(X, O_X(nD)) is a quadratic polynomial in n with leading term determined by (D·D) (Asymptotic Riemann–Roch remark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relates intersection theory to Riemann–Roch on surfaces and shows how intersection pairing encodes growth of Euler characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjunction formula and Riemann–Roch for surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: On a smooth projective surface X (assuming Serre duality): (a) adjunction: C·(C + K_X) = 2 p_a(C) − 2 for any curve C ⊂ X; (b) Riemann–Roch for surfaces: χ(X, O_X(D)) = (D·(D − K_X))/2 + χ(X, O_X) for any Weil divisor D (Exercise 20.2.B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two formulas are central tools for computations on surfaces; hints: use Serre duality and prior intersection properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete examples: intersection matrices for P1×P1 and blow-up Bl_p P2
rubrics_metrics.description: On X = P1 × P1, Pic ≅ Z·ℓ ⊕ Z·m with intersection ℓ·m = 1, ℓ·ℓ = m·m = 0. For the blow-up X = Bl_p P2, Pic is generated by ℓ (proper transform of a line) and e (exceptional divisor) with intersection numbers ℓ·ℓ = 1, e·e = −1, ℓ·e = 0 (Exercises 20.2.C and 20.2.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute via proper transforms and scheme-theoretic preimages; these examples illustrate negative self-intersection of exceptional divisors and how blow-ups change intersection form.
